Being Transgender

By: Nicola De Chaud | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Being transgender - what does it mean, and what is it like to live

Unique Selling Point:
Being trans is a generally misunderstood lifestyle. It's current, it's edgy, it's curious and it's mostly kept under the covers - we blow the covers back!

Summary:
Life is tough for most of us - in one way or another. The struggle for identity, for belonging, for purpose and community is mired into every life journey. For those who live outside of social averages and accepted norms the struggle is measureless.

ELLE, a young transgender woman faces a relentless battle for identity every day.

Elle is one the fortunate ones. She comes from a tolerant family, who understood from very early on, that she was more girl than boy. She says that growing up, she was gender fluid, and had a supportive space within which to explore her identity. Elle is making her way as a successful model and is an activist in the trans space in South Africa.

SIYA born male, is a trans woman who was thrown out of her home at an early age because she identified female. She moves from shelter to shelter and is often ejected through fear and ignorance. Siya is homeless and without family, but in spite of the daily onslaught on her personhood, she has achieved remarkable things. She has a degree in architecture and is studying towards her masters. It’s bittersweet, since Siya can’t get a job while her born identity mismatches her chosen gender fit. The admin precludes her.

These are some of the difficult things trans gender people face in South Africa.
We explore the lived experience of being trans up close and personal through the experiences of Elle and Siya and their immediate social group. We get a broader perspective from Jabu at Iranti – an advocacy organization working with trans rights in Africa and we talk to a psychologist about the particular complications of being trans in a hetero-normative world.

Press Release:


Being Transgender
Transgender is a little understood identity and for some, coming to terms with being a trans person, is the struggle of a lifetime. Elle and Siya often face difficult questions about their gender identities, but they believe that being transgender is the ultimate expression of living. Carte Blanche explores how these women are helping to break the stereotype.


Script:


Elle: What is a real girl? What does that mean? So like, my thing is like, what is your definition of that because that’s very subjective.

VO: Cis gender, trans man, gay, straight, queer, binary, polygender, trans woman, gender fluid – a profusion labels, a confusion of identifications.

Siya: I felt trapped in this identity that society gives you that you are born a boy, so you are a boy, but why do I not feel like a boy? You know my soul, my spirit, everything that I embrace I enjoy, tells me that I am female.

VO: In South Africa, our constitution allows for individuals to change their identity and assign themselves a preferred gender

Link: But on the ground, the lived experience of transgender people is quite another thing.

Elle: I think that there is a rejection of trance people not because of religion but just a general lack of understanding of what it means to be trans gender. A lot of people assume that its this idea that you are changing what you are to become something else and I think that’s where people’s initial reservations lie, whereas for trans people it’s almost the opposite, it’s like we’re asserting our identities and identifying ourselves as how we’ve always been.

Jabu: I think we all know we are born human, that is the only human fact we know.

VO: Jabu PERRIERA heads up Iranti a trans, lesbian, intersex human rights organization which focuses on education about being transgender

Jabu: to start off sexuality is about who you love, so you could be gay, bisexual heterosexual. Gender identity is how you express yourself daily

Elle: I grew up not having the vocabulary to express my gender identity. I didn’t know what a trans person was,. So I think in early years, like in preschool, with boys and girls all growing up and there’s no physical distinguishable difference in you. I always just thought I was one of the girls.

VO: Elle was born Luke 19 years ago and remembers the boy child as flamboyant and creative.

Elle: I wasn’t interested in climbing trees or wrestling, like that stuff didn’t interest me, um boys were gross to me, eeu icky. There were moments when I felt isolated and different, so there’s like the rule like, girls line up in this line and boys in that line. Growing up that’s when I started noticing it, if I reflect back, those things made me uncomfortable.

Edwina: I think it was quite obvious and apparent that he wasn’t like any other boy

VO: Elle’s mother Edwina says she always knew that Luke was something other.

Edwina: My kid had a different personality and was a different type of child and ja I kind of just let him be him from a very early age.

VO: Siya Hlongwa also expressed herself female from very early on

Siya: As I got older and older as Siyabonga, the boy I would sit there in front of the television and start singing and my grandmother would walk into the room, and I remember this one particular day, when she walked in and caught me standing in front of the television set and starting to dance along with the tune and what not, and singing and she’s like Ahh! My goodness and I’m like “whats up gran” “Youre a girl!” Im like Duh, hello!”

VO: Luke first encountered the term transgender in the media as a teen and it fitted. It took some time before she was able to come out and openly express herself as a transgender woman to friends and family.

Elle: There’s always like this thing in the back of your mind. You hear horror stories. You hear about kids getting isolated and put on the streets and murdered, but their families. That was something that I didn’t expect to happen, but was like in the back of my mind.

Edwina: I was taken aback initially by my own … I knew I was fine with her saying it to me that she was transgender, I knew it was coming. I had sense before she actually made that announcement, my immediate reaction is phew! Here we go now we can actually start dealing with this from a perspective of authenticity. But there was also a kind of reticence in me from a mothers perspective and a big part of it which I had to unpack was around fear

VO: Siya faced violence and rejection from people closest to her.

Siya: for me I honestly came to a space where I wanted to just die.

VO She was regularly threatened by a male member of the family and left home in KZN to find her own way.

Siya: I think for a lot of trans people you have to move out of home to be able to exercise you true identity as a trans person.

Link: Siya moved to Johannesburg in 2011 with a degree in architecture from UKZN. Since then, she has struggled to find work in her field as a trans woman.

Siya: People interview me and then there’s the discrepancy of Mr Siyabonga Hlongwa, and in walks this lady in high heels… with a five o-clock shadow and then the opportunity is gone ‘cause they think ok this person is a clown, this person is illiterate, this person is a hoax, this person is a con artist

VO: Jobless and homeless, Siya has been exposed to the worst of the big city.

Siya: I come to this big city and I have always seen myself as this woman, but now I am raped. Someone took advantage of me and forced themselves on me and that’s when I discovered there was even such a term as transgender. I always thought that I was the only one.

VO: After her sexual assault, Siya found help through Iranti.

Jabu: She’s not a victim, she’s a survivor. She is an incredibly resilient young woman and she faces prejudice all the time.

VO: Always an outsider, Siya has to fight for her place in the world.

Jabu: She is homeless, at the moment she doesn’t have a place to stay.

VO: Despite being on the streets, Siya is doing her masters degree on a bursary in town planning at Wits

Siya: And so I am struggling you know having to sleep in lecture rooms, having to sleep under the tables, you wait for everyone to leave… people are gone home just dive under the desk and take an nap, put your jacket over your face and take a nap. Cause I live in lecture rooms and libraries.. That’s my home right now cause I cant afford anywhere else. And even the blanket I use at night is a donation from the cleaners. And it breaks me.. It breaks me because there’s no dignity in that, there’s no humanity in that, and it’s sad that we live in a world where I have to face that everyday

Edwina: In an ideal world my child will never have to face animosity misogyny, violence but you know we don’t live in an ideal world. Myy parting words to ha=r always is goodbye be safe

Elle: I’m scared everyday to be honest, because I never know what peoples reaction to me existing are.. Whether someone is just going to say something verbally, or physically. It hasn’t happened yet but that’s always in the back of my mind. Like what if I’m just going to the bathroom and someone follows me and no one can hear me screaming.

VO: Jabu Perrera says violence against transwomen in South Africa is rife. Murder and suicide rates in this community are unusually high.

Jabu: Just because of the extent of violence that they face, not just within the system, but in the public sphere which leads a lot to depression and forces trans people to live in isolation.

VO: Siya seldom moves off campus. She lives off of food parcels from the university and with a little help from Iranti

Jabu: She’s one of those people as South Africans who we look at and have to say, this is what resilience looks like. This is how you push against transphobia, this is how you push against a system and you keep going.

Siya: I choose to fight, at least most of the time and my fighting is in my academics, you know

VO: Siya is a top student, but despite her academic achievements, continues to feel ‘othered”

Elle: People are not only living with fear but with a sense of invalidation of themselves. The have to wake up and look at themselves everyday and feel scared or dysphoric or worried about their bodies

VO: Elle would like to support her bodily transition with hormone replacement therapy

Elle: At the moment I’m trying to find an endocrinologist to test me. Then it’s a lot of trial and error. How much do I need to take to start seeing substantial changes. It’s about finding people who are willing to treat you and treat you safely.

Siya: I need, I desperately need to get access to avoid the stereotypes that society inflicts on people

Elle: We are not getting these procedures to make ourselves look better, but rather to make ourselves safer. So that when we are walking on the street people don’t go there’s a trans person, lets get them!

VO: Once Elle and Siya access hormone therapy, they would be eligible for gender reassignment surgery

Elle: Ive been tossing it up. A big question is why should I have to medicalize my identity, for who? It doesn’t make sense to me because I’m not walking around with my pants off, like to really shouldn’t matter to anybody

VO: Outspoken and spirited at 19 Elle is a successful model and is taking on transgender issues from a strong position of privilege.

Elle: I cant imagine what it’s like when you need to get your education, work to put food on the table. I have to remind myself everyday how privileged I am because my experience is not the general experience.

Siya: What I’m scared of is that I just don’t want to die in this position having never accessed a normal life, just shelter, just food, just a job, just the right to be called who I really am; Ms Siya Hlongwa.
